title: The call of the king
hook: the second week: Christ calls, and you ask to follow closely

segments.voice: Yesterday, imagine the scene: Ignatius put you on the Jericho road. Your line was step into the story. Which ordinary moment did you take in with every sense? Day one thousand one hundred forty-three.

A king stands before his people and makes an offer. He's setting out on a hard campaign. Whoever comes with him will eat what he eats and wear what he wears. They'll work beside him by day and keep watch with him by night. They'll share the hardship, and then they'll share the victory. Ignatius of Loyola sets that scene at the start of the second week of his Spiritual Exercises. He asks the one praying to picture a good human leader calling like that, and to ask what a decent person would answer. Then he turns the picture around. If that's how people would answer an earthly king, what about Christ? Today: the call of the king.

In the Gospels, a call can be very short. Jesus walks by the Sea of Galilee, sees Simon and Andrew casting a net, and says, in the King James words: "Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men." And the next line: "And they straightway left their nets, and followed him." No speech, no terms. Ignatius slows that moment down. In his meditation, Christ the king calls the whole world, and each person one by one, to share his work and his hardship, so as to share his glory. Then Ignatius describes the answers. Anyone with judgment, he says, would offer themselves for the work. But some will want to go further and offer more: to follow Christ even in bearing wrongs and in poverty, if that's where he leads. Notice the shape of that bigger answer. It isn't a boast. It's a request. From here on, the grace Ignatius has people ask for in the second week runs close to this: to know Jesus more from the inside, to love him more, and to follow him more closely. Know, love, follow, in that order. It's hard to follow well someone you've only heard about. That's why what comes next in the Exercises is a run of gospel stories: the birth, the hidden years, the baptism, the calls by the lake. The one praying watches Jesus up close before deciding anything. Christians have prayed that same desire in other words. An old English prayer, which tradition gives to Richard of Chichester, asks to see him more clearly, love him more dearly, and follow him more nearly. Today's line borrows its end. Following more nearly isn't a leap into heroics. It's one step closer than yesterday.

Here's the practice: ask to follow more closely. Settle and breathe. Use yesterday's way in: stand by the lake. The water, the boats, a wet net in your hands. Hear the call, short and plain. Then notice what rises. Eagerness, maybe. Hesitation. A list of reasons this isn't a good time. Don't fix any of it. If you pray, you can ask, in your own words, to know him more, love him more, and follow him more nearly. If you don't pray, notice one thing you'd want to move a step closer to. The bell holds the time.
The call of the king. Ignatius' meditation that opens the second week: Christ calls each person to share his work, and the generous answer asks to follow him more closely.

segments.voice: Your line: to follow more nearly. Today, pick one small step toward what matters most to you, and take it before dinner. Day one thousand one hundred forty-three.

fork.setup: in Ignatius' meditation, the king calls companions to share his hardship and then his victory. what answer is Ignatius hoping for?
options: say it sounds good, and stay home.
offer to work, and ask to follow more closely still.
wait for the victory, then join.
fork.reveal: Ignatius says anyone with judgment would offer to work. the more generous answer asks to follow even more closely, wherever that leads.

notes: Paraphrases the Call of the Temporal King: eat, drink and dress as the king, labor by day and watch by night, share the hardship and the victory; those with judgment offer themselves for the labor; the more generous offer to imitate Christ in bearing injuries and poverty. Confirm.
The second-week grace (interior knowledge of the Lord, to love him more and follow him more closely) is paraphrased; confirm.

The prayer 'see thee more clearly, love thee more dearly, follow thee more nearly' is attributed to Richard of Chichester by tradition; its familiar wording is a later form. Paraphrased, not quoted. Confirm the attribution phrasing.
The list of Second Week contemplations (birth, hidden years, baptism, calls by the lake) is a summary; confirm.
Editor: 'The Gospels are full of calls, and they're short' (a sweeping claim) changed to 'In the Gospels, a call can be very short', resting on the Matthew 4 text quoted.
